arXiv:2602.04448v1 [cs.LG] 04 Feb 2026

RASA: Routing-Aware Safety Alignment for Mixture-of-Experts Models

Jiacheng Liang Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, USA    Yuhui Wang Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, USA    Tanqiu Jiang Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, USA    Ting Wang Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, USA Correspondence to: twang@cs.stonybrook.edu
Abstract

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models introduce unique challenges for safety alignment due to their sparse routing mechanisms, which can enable degenerate optimization behaviors under standard full-parameter fine-tuning. In our preliminary experiments, we observe that naively applying full-parameter safety fine-tuning to MoE models can reduce attack success rates through routing or expert dominance effects, rather than by directly repairing Safety-Critical Experts. To address this challenge, we propose RASA, a routing-aware expert-level alignment framework that explicitly repairs Safety-Critical Experts while preventing routing-based bypasses. RASA identifies experts disproportionately activated by successful jailbreaks, selectively fine-tunes only these experts under fixed routing, and subsequently enforces routing consistency with safety-aligned contexts. Across two representative MoE architectures and a diverse set of jailbreak attacks, RASA achieves near-perfect robustness, strong cross-attack generalization, and substantially reduced over-refusal, while preserving general capabilities on benchmarks such as MMLU, GSM8K, and TruthfulQA. Our results suggest that robust MoE safety alignment benefits from targeted expert repair rather than global parameter updates, offering a practical and architecture-preserving alternative to prior approaches. The code is available at: https://github.com/JACKPURCELL/RASAMoE-public.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models (Muennighoff et al., 2025; Artetxe et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2025a) introduce new challenges for safety alignment due to their unique mechanisms, which route each input through only a small subset of experts. While this architectural flexibility improves scalability and efficiency, it also enables failure modes absent in dense models. In our preliminary experiments, we consistently observe that end-to-end safety fine-tuning on MoE models can improve attack harmlessness rates by amplifying already-safe experts or biasing the router toward conservative routing patterns, while leaving certain experts uncorrected. As a result, apparent safety improvements may be achieved without directly repairing the experts responsible for unsafe behaviors, leaving latent vulnerabilities exploitable under adaptive adversarial prompts.

We refer to this empirically observed failure pattern as an alignment shortcut in MoE safety training in Figure 1. Rather than explicitly correcting the parameters associated with unsafe behaviors, full-parameter alignment may admit shortcut solutions in which safety objectives are satisfied through routing or expert dominance effects, without meaningful expert-level repair. Empirically, this behavior is associated with two recurring failure modes: (i) Safety-Critical Experts remain uncorrected and can be reactivated by unseen or adaptive jailbreak strategies, and (ii) already-safe(remaining) experts become increasingly dominant, leading to excessive refusals and degraded general capabilities. Similar shortcut-like behaviors have been reported in other safety settings, where shallow alignment objectives yield brittle and poorly generalizable defenses (Qi et al., 2025a; Wei et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024).

In this work, we argue that robust safety alignment for MoE models requires explicitly repairing Safety-Critical Experts instead of bypassing them. We propose RASA, a targeted expert-level alignment framework that prevents alignment shortcuts by disentangling expert correction from routing control. Our method first identifies Safety-Critical Experts based on activation discrepancies between safe and adversarial contexts, selectively fine-tunes only these experts under fixed routing, and subsequently optimizes the router to maintain consistency with safe routing patterns. This design ensures that safety supervision reaches the parameters responsible for unsafe behavior, while preserving the contributions of benign experts and the original MoE architecture.

Instead of allowing unsafe inputs to be silently rerouted or absorbed by over-aligned safe experts, our framework enforces explicit correction of Safety-Critical Experts and prevents their activation from being bypassed. This results in a form of defense-in-depth: unsafe behaviors are suppressed at their source, while routing behavior remains stable and interpretable.

Extensive experiments on two representative MoE architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. RASA consistently achieves near-perfect defense against diverse jailbreak attacks, substantially improves cross-attack generalization, and significantly reduces over-refusal compared to full-parameter alignment and prior MoE-specific methods. Moreover, our method is highly data-efficient, achieving strong safety gains with only a fraction of adversarial samples, and preserves general performance across benchmarks such as MMLU, GSM8K, and TruthfulQA.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We empirically observe a recurring failure pattern when applying full-parameter safety alignment to MoE models, where safety objectives can be satisfied without directly correcting experts responsible for unsafe behaviors. We refer to this phenomenon as an alignment shortcut.

  • •

    We propose RASA, a targeted expert-level alignment framework that repairs Safety-Critical Experts while preventing routing-based shortcut solutions.

  • •

    We demonstrate strong robustness to diverse jailbreak attacks, controlled over-refusal, and preserved general capabilities across architectures.

2 Related Work

Safety Alignment in Dense Language Models. Safety alignment has been primarily studied in dense models via supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and preference-based optimization such as DPO (Bai et al., 2022; Ouyang et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023). While effective at suppressing overtly unsafe outputs, these methods often rely on surface-level refusal behaviors and remain vulnerable to adaptive prompt-based jailbreak attacks (Zou et al., 2023; Chao et al., 2024; Qi et al., 2025a; Wei et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Liang et al., 2025a). These limitations motivate alignment strategies that intervene at the level of internal model mechanisms.

Expert-Level Steering and Attacks in MoE Models. Several works analyze expert activations to localize safety-relevant components in MoE models. SteerMoE (Fayyaz et al., 2025) suppresses unsafe experts at inference time by modifying routing logits, but does not update expert parameters or repair unsafe representations. GateBreaker (Wu et al., 2025) further shows that MoE safety often concentrates in a small subset of experts or neurons and can be bypassed by directly manipulating expert execution. However, such attacks assume access to model internals, whereas we focus on the strictly harder and more realistic prompt-only threat model and address the training-time causes of such brittle safety concentration.

Architecture-Modifying MoE Alignment. Another line of work improves safety by introducing auxiliary experts or explicit expert roles. SafeX (Lai et al., 2025), SafeMoE-LoRAExpert (Anonymous submission to ICLR; manuscript currently unavailable), and MidPO (Qi et al., 2025b) construct specialized safety-related experts (e.g., via LoRA or preference optimization) and rely on routing mechanisms to balance safety and utility. While effective in structured settings, these approaches modify the original model composition or routing semantics and do not address whether safety supervision truly repairs the experts responsible for unsafe behavior, leaving routing-based shortcut solutions unexamined.

Routing Regularization and Redesign. Routing-focused approaches aim to stabilize or reshape expert activation patterns. SafeMoE-Fine-tuning (Anonymous, 2025) constrains routing distributions to remain close to a safe anchor, while EMoE (Cheng et al., 2026) redesigns the router to mitigate expert dominance and redundancy. These methods improve routing behavior but do not directly target safety alignment or prevent routing from absorbing safety supervision while unsafe experts remain uncorrected.

Understanding Expert Specialization. Recent analyses study how routing and expert specialization emerge in MoE models. Multilingual MoE studies (Chen et al., 2026) and MoTE (Liu et al., 2025) show that expert activation exhibits structured and consistent patterns across inputs and layers. While providing useful context for expert-level analysis, these works do not study safety alignment failures or routing-based shortcut optimization under adversarial prompts.

Our Positioning. In contrast to prior work, we identify a training-time failure mode specific to MoE safety alignment shortcuts, where full-parameter fine-tuning reduces apparent risk through routing or expert dominance effects without repairing unsafe experts. We propose a routing-aware expert-level alignment framework that explicitly repairs Safety-Critical Experts under fixed routing and only subsequently enforces routing consistency. Our approach introduces no auxiliary experts, requires no architectural modification, and performs no inference-time intervention, achieving robust defense against prompt-only jailbreak attacks within the original MoE structure.

3 RASA

We propose a dual-layered safety alignment framework for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. Our approach first dynamically identifies “Safety-Critical Experts” at the batch level based on activation discrepancies and subsequently optimizes the model through an alternating strategy that combines selective fine-tuning with routing consistency. The pseudo-code is provided in Algorithm 1.

3.1 Preliminaries and Notation

Consider an MoE model ℳ\mathcal{M} with LL layers. Each layer l∈{1,…,L}l\in\{1,\dots,L\} contains a set of EE experts {El,e}e=1E\{E_{l,e}\}_{e=1}^{E} and a routing function GlG_{l}. For an input token xx, the router selects the top-kk experts to process the token. Let Hl,e​(x)∈{0,1}H_{l,e}(x)\in\{0,1\} be the binary indicator of whether expert ee in layer ll is activated for token xx. We denote the parameters of all experts as Θ\Theta and the router parameters as Φ\Phi. The notation table can be found in Table  5.

3.2 A Bi-level Optimization Formulation

In sparse MoE models, jointly optimizing router and expert parameters can allow safety loss to be minimized through routing behavior alone, preventing Safety-Critical Experts from being properly updated. To prevent such shortcut solutions, we decouple expert alignment from routing optimization and cast our method as a bi-level optimization problem. Formally,

minΦ⁡𝔼ℬ​[ℒrouter​(Φ,arg⁡minΘ​ℒSFT​(Θ,Φ))]\min_{\Phi}{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathcal{B}}[{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{router}}(\Phi;\arg\min_{\Theta}{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{SFT}}(\Theta,\Phi))] (1)

where the inner problem ℒSFT{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{SFT}} selectively fine-tunes Safety-Critical Experts identified based on adversarial activation discrepancy, while the outer problem ℒrouter{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{router}} optimizes routing behavior given aligned experts.

3.3 Alternating Optimization Strategy

Direct differentiation through the inner optimization is impractical due to the scale and sparsity of MoE architectures and the batch-dependent nature of unsafe expert identification. We adopt an alternating strategy that approximates the bi-level objective via block-coordinate descent, freezing routers during expert alignment and freezing expert parameters during router optimization. Despite its simplicity, this procedure effectively couples expert specialization and routing behavior through shared activation statistics.

3.3.1 Inner Optimization: Selective Expert Fine-tuning (SFT)

The inner optimization phase consists of two steps: (i) identifying Safety-Critical Experts that are disproportionately activated by successful jailbreak prompts, and (ii) selectively fine-tuning only these experts under fixed routing to inject refusal behavior, while leaving benign experts unaffected.

Mixed Batch Construction.

Each training batch ℬ=ℬa​n​c​h​o​r∪ℬa​d​v\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{B}_{anchor}\cup\mathcal{B}_{adv} is constructed by pairing prompts that share the same underlying malicious intent but differ in surface form. Let ℐ\mathcal{I} denote a set of harmful intents. For each intent i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}, we construct:

  • •

    Anchor Prompts (ℬa​n​c​h​o​r\mathcal{B}_{anchor}): original malicious prompts for which the current model produces a refusal or a safety-aligned response, serving as a reference context.

  • •

    Adversarial Prompts (ℬa​d​v\mathcal{B}_{adv}): jailbreak-modified variants of the same intents that successfully bypass safety mechanisms and elicit non-refusal responses.

To prevent label noise from failed or partially effective jailbreaks, we re-evaluate model responses at each training round and retain only prompt pairs whose outcomes match our definitions: the anchor prompt must elicit a safety-aligned response, while its paired adversarial prompt must successfully bypass safety and elicit a non-refusal response. If either side fails to satisfy the criterion, we discard the entire pair, ensuring a one-to-one correspondence between ℬanchor\mathcal{B}_{\text{anchor}} and ℬadv\mathcal{B}_{\text{adv}} throughout training.

Identifying Safety-Critical Experts.

To quantify expert sensitivity to jailbreak perturbations, we measure the discrepancy between its activation frequency under adversarial and anchor contexts. For each expert (l,e)(l,e), we define the Adversarial Activation Discrepancy (AAD) as:

Δl,e=ℙ⁡(activel,e∣ℬa​d​v)−ℙ⁡(activel,e∣ℬa​n​c​h​o​r),\Delta_{l,e}=\mathbb{P}(\text{active}_{l,e}\mid\mathcal{B}_{adv})-\mathbb{P}(\text{active}_{l,e}\mid\mathcal{B}_{anchor}), (2)

where

ℙ⁡(activel,e∣𝒳)=1|𝒳|​∑x∈𝒳Hl,e​(x),\mathbb{P}(\text{active}_{l,e}\mid\mathcal{X})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{X}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}H_{l,e}(x), (3)

and Hl,e​(x)∈{0,1}H_{l,e}(x)\in\{0,1\} indicates whether expert (l,e)(l,e) is activated for input xx.

A high Δl,e\Delta_{l,e} indicates that the expert is disproportionately activated by prompts that successfully bypass safety mechanisms, relative to prompts that are correctly refused. Such experts are therefore considered safety-critical.

For each training batch bb, we dynamically identify the set of Safety-Critical Experts by thresholding the adversarial activation discrepancy:

ℰcrit(b)={(l,e)∣Δl,e>τ},\mathcal{E}_{\text{crit}}^{(b)}=\{(l,e)\mid\Delta_{l,e}>\tau\}, (4)

where τ\tau controls the number of experts selected for expert-level alignment.

Selective Expert Fine-tuning.

Given the identified set of Safety-Critical Experts ℰcrit(b)\mathcal{E}_{\text{crit}}^{(b)}, we fix the router parameters Φ\Phi and selectively update only the corresponding expert parameters. The trainable expert parameters are defined as

Θcrit={θl,e∣(l,e)∈ℰcrit(b)},\Theta_{\text{crit}}=\{\theta_{l,e}\mid(l,e)\in\mathcal{E}_{\text{crit}}^{(b)}\},

while all remaining expert parameters are kept frozen. The goal is to inject refusal behavior into experts that are disproportionately involved in processing jailbreak-specific activations, without perturbing experts responsible for benign reasoning.

With routing fixed as Φ\Phi, we define the inner optimization objective as:

Θ∗​(Φ)=arg⁡minΘcrit​𝔼(x,yref)∼𝒟a​d​v​[ℒSFT​(x,yref,Θcrit,Φ)]\hskip-15.0pt\Theta^{*}(\Phi)=\arg\min_{\Theta_{\text{crit}}}\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_{\text{ref}})\sim\mathcal{D}_{adv}}\left[\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}(x,y_{\text{ref}};\Theta_{\text{crit}},\Phi)\right] (5)

where xx denotes an adversarial prompt and yrefy_{\text{ref}} is a safety-aligned refusal response. To avoid overfitting to a single refusal template, we generate diverse refusal responses using an external language model, encouraging experts to internalize refusal behavior at the representation level rather than memorizing surface patterns.

We instantiate ℒSFT\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}} as the standard cross-entropy loss:

ℒSFT(x,yref;Θcrit,Φ)=−∑tlogP(yt∣y<t,x;Θcrit,Φ)\hskip-15.0pt\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}(x,y_{\text{ref}};\Theta_{\text{crit}},\Phi)=-\sum_{t}\log P(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},x;\Theta_{\text{crit}},\Phi) (6)

By restricting gradient updates to ℰcrit(b)\mathcal{E}_{\text{crit}}^{(b)}, we precisely inject refusal behavior into Safety-Critical Experts associated with jailbreak-specific activations, while leaving the remaining experts unchanged.

3.3.2 Outer Optimization: Router Consistency

Given the solution of the inner optimization Θ∗​(Φ)\Theta^{*}(\Phi), we define the outer objective as:

minΦ⁡𝔼ℬ​[ℒrouter​(Φ,Θ∗​(Φ))].\min_{\Phi}\;\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{B}}\big[\mathcal{L}_{\text{router}}(\Phi;\Theta^{*}(\Phi))\big]. (7)

The goal of this phase is to prevent adversarial inputs from activating Safety-Critical Experts by adjusting routing behavior, while preserving stable routing patterns for safety-aligned contexts. To this end, we optimize the router parameters Φ\Phi while keeping all expert parameters Θ\Theta frozen.

Double-Forward Routing Strategy.

We employ a double-forward strategy that decouples safe routing anchors from adversarial routing optimization:

  • •

    Anchor Forward (No Gradient). We compute the mean routing distribution induced by anchor prompts ℬa​n​c​h​o​r\mathcal{B}_{anchor} without gradient updates:

    p¯a​n​c​h​o​r(l)=sg​(1|ℬa​n​c​h​o​r|​∑x∈ℬa​n​c​h​o​rsoftmax​(zl​(x))),\bar{p}_{anchor}^{(l)}=\text{sg}\!\left(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{anchor}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{B}_{anchor}}\text{softmax}(z_{l}(x))\right),

    where zl​(x)z_{l}(x) denotes the router logits at layer ll and sg​[⋅]\text{sg}[\cdot] is the stop-gradient operator.

  • •

    Adversarial Forward (Trainable). We compute the routing distribution for adversarial prompts ℬa​d​v\mathcal{B}_{adv} with gradients enabled:

    p¯a​d​v(l)​(Φ)=1|ℬa​d​v|​∑x∈ℬa​d​vsoftmax​(zl​(x,Φ)).\bar{p}_{adv}^{(l)}(\Phi)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{adv}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{B}_{adv}}\text{softmax}(z_{l}(x;\Phi)).
Routing Consistency Loss.

The router is optimized to align the adversarial routing distribution with the anchor routing reference via a forward KL divergence:

ℒrouter(Φ)=1L∑l=1LDKL(p¯a​n​c​h​o​r(l)∥p¯a​d​v(l)(Φ)).\mathcal{L}_{\text{router}}(\Phi)=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\bar{p}_{anchor}^{(l)}\,\|\,\bar{p}_{adv}^{(l)}(\Phi)\right). (8)

This objective encourages adversarial inputs to follow routing patterns consistent with safety-aligned contexts, thereby reducing their likelihood of activating Safety-Critical Experts without introducing degenerate routing shortcuts.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Models and Datasets. We evaluate two representative MoE architectures: Qwen3-30B-A3B (Yang et al., 2025a) and OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct (Muennighoff et al., 2025). For safety training and evaluation, we use AdvBench  (Zou et al., 2023) as the core intent set. To create adversarial counterparts, we employ state-of-the-art (SOTA) jailbreak attacks to generate Adversarial Prompts (ℬa​d​v\mathcal{B}_{adv}), ensuring the attacks successfully bypass the original models’ initial safety filters before alignment.

Baselines. We compare our method against two primary baselines:

  • •

    Original Model: The original instruction-tuned MoE model from the distributors.

  • •

    SteerMoE (Fayyaz et al., 2025): An activation-based inference-time steering approach that identifies experts with high activation discrepancy under unsafe prompts and suppresses their routing logits at inference time, without performing parameter updates or expert-level repair.

Jailbreak Methods We considered various jailbreak methods in the currect survey  (Chu et al., 2025), including FlipAttack (Liu et al., 2024b), DeepInception (Li et al., 2023), and Persuasion (Zeng et al., 2024), all of which demonstrated relatively high attack success rates (ASR) under the current MoE model. Consequently, we selected these three methods as the primary attack strategies for our analysis. Other methods, such as DevMode v2 (Albert & Team, 2025), AIM (Albert & Team, 2025), PAIR (Chao et al., 2024) and AutoDAN-Turbo (Liu et al., 2024a) , were also considered but exhibited either lower ASR or substantially longer execution time compared to the selected methods. We present the attack success rates of these methods in Table  6.

Evaluation Metrics. We assess the models across three dimensions:

  • •

    Harmlessness: We report the Harmlessness Rate on both original harmful prompts(StrongReject (Souly et al., 2024)) and specific jailbreak vectors(based on AdvBench (Zou et al., 2023)), where a higher value indicates stronger safety alignment. Following the LLM-related research (Yang et al., 2025b; Ji et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2024; Tian & Wang, 2025; Liang et al., 2025b), harmlessness is automatically judged by GPT-4o-mini, with the full judging prompt and criteria are provided in Appendix C.

  • •

    General Utility: To ensure that alignment does not degrade model performance, following the related work (Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025a; Jiang et al., 2024), we evaluate on general benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, MMLU).

  • •

    Over-refusal: We use the over-refusal subset of XsTest  (Röttger et al., 2024) to measure the over-refusal rate, ensuring the model remains helpful for sensitive queries.

4.2 Main Results: Defense Against Diverse Attacks

We evaluate our method on representative jailbreak attacks across both OLMoE and Qwen architectures. Table 1 summarizes model performance under different jailbreak settings. SteerMoE yields marginal improvements in harmlessness with negligible impact on general capability and over-refusal, consistent with its inference-time expert suppression design. In contrast, RASA achieves substantial gains under both individual and mixed attacks by explicitly repairing Safety-Critical Experts. We also provide evaluation results of each round in Figure  3(a).

Targeted Expert Alignment Yields Near-Perfect Safety on Aligned Attacks. Across both OLMoE and Qwen, expert-level alignment guided by safety-critical expert identification consistently achieves near-perfect harmlessness on the aligned jailbreak category. In all targeted settings, the corresponding attack-specific safety score reaches or approaches 1.0, while StrongReject and XsTest (should refuse subset) remain stable. These results indicate that jailbreak vulnerabilities in MoE models are highly localized and can be effectively neutralized by selectively repairing a small subset of experts, without relying on global parameter updates.

Cross-Attack Generalization Emerges Without Multi-Attack Supervision. Beyond the aligned attack, we observe consistent improvements on other, unseen jailbreak methods. Aligning on a single attack category often reduces vulnerability across multiple attack dimensions, suggesting that different jailbreak strategies partially share underlying Safety-Critical Experts. Correcting these experts therefore removes common adversarial pathways, leading to broader robustness without explicit multi-attack training.

Safety Gains Preserve General Capability and Avoid Over-Refusal. Crucially, the safety improvements do not come at the cost of general utility. Performance on MMLU, GSM8K, and TruthfulQA remains stable or slightly improves across all targeted settings. At the same time, over-refusal remains controlled: aligned models maintain near-perfect XsTest (correct) scores and avoid collapsing into indiscriminate refusal. This confirms that confining updates to Safety-Critical Experts enables fine-grained safety control while preserving the model’s general reasoning abilities.

4.3 Mixed-Attack Alignment

We further evaluate our framework under a mixed-attack setting, where training batches combine samples from multiple jailbreak strategies (FlipAttack, DeepInception, and Persuasion).

As shown in Table 1, mixed-attack alignment achieves near-perfect defense across all evaluated jailbreaks. Qwen reaches a harmlessness score of 1.0 on all attack vectors, while OLMoE achieves perfect defense on FlipAttack and DeepInception and 0.98 on Persuasion. Importantly, these gains are achieved without degrading general performance or inducing excessive refusal.

These results demonstrate that our framework naturally supports multi-attack alignment: Safety-Critical Experts shared across different jailbreak strategies can be jointly identified and corrected, enabling unified and robust defense rather than attack-specific overfitting.

4.4 Multi-turn Jailbreak Defense.

We additionally evaluate our method under a challenging multi-turn jailbreak setting using X-Teaming (Rahman et al., 2025), a recent red-teaming framework designed to study how harmful intent can be gradually introduced and escalated across multiple conversational turns. Unlike single-turn attacks, X-Teaming leverages collaborative agents for planning, attack optimization, and verification, enabling diverse and effective multi-turn jailbreak trajectories.

In our evaluation, we use X-Teaming to generate multi-turn attack dialogues against the model. For alignment, we replace the final assistant response within each successful jailbreak trajectory with a safety-aligned refusal response, using these for expert-level fine-tuning. Table 2 summarizes the results under the multi-turn X-Teaming setting. After alignment , the model maintains comparable general performance and an unchanged over-refusal rate relative to the original model. At the same time, the X-Teaming safety rate increases from 0.00.0 to 0.20.2, indicating improved robustness to multi-turn jailbreak attempts without introducing negative side effects on general behavior.

5 Ablation Study

5.1 Impact of Expert Selection Ratio (Top-kk)

We analyze how the number of selected Safety-Critical Experts affects safety, general utility, and over-refusal behavior. Instead of defining top-kk as a fixed percentage, we vary the absolute number of experts ranked by activation discrepancy Δl,e\Delta_{l,e}, which better reflects practical deployment across heterogeneous MoE architectures. Figure 3(b) summarizes the performance trends, while Table 4 provides a layer-wise interpretation of the selected ranges.

Across both OLMoE and Qwen, we observe a consistent pattern: increasing top-kk initially improves safety, but overly aggressive selection degrades general performance and increases over-refusal. This indicates a clear optimal region in which Safety-Critical Experts are sufficiently covered without unnecessarily modifying benign experts.

For OLMoE, moderate top-kk values achieve the best balance between robustness and utility. Smaller selections underfit safety alignment, while larger selections begin to harm general performance. For Qwen, effective safety alignment requires selecting a larger number of experts due to its deeper architecture and higher expert capacity.

Taken together, these results indicate that selecting approximately 10%–15% of experts per layer yields the best balance between safety and general utility across architectures.

5.2 Data Scaling and Attack Sample Requirements

We evaluate how the amount of adversarial data affects alignment performance by varying the fraction of available jailbreak samples used for training. Figure 3(c) reports results under different data ratios for both OLMoE and Qwen across multiple attack types.

Overall, alignment performance remains largely stable as the amount of training data decreases. In most settings, using 25%25\%–50%50\% of the available attack samples already achieves comparable current-attack harmlessness and average harmlessness to the full-data configuration, without introducing systematic increases in over-refusal or degradation in general performance.

While some attack- and model-specific fluctuations are observed under stronger attacks such as Persuasion, the overall trend indicates that effective safety alignment can be achieved with a limited number of successful jailbreak samples. These results highlight RASA’s data efficiency and suggest its practicality in real-world deployment scenarios where large-scale adversarial data may be unavailable.

5.3 Phase Balancing: Expert vs. Router Epochs

We study the impact of balancing expert fine-tuning and router optimization by varying the ratio between expert epochs (Es​f​tE_{sft}) and router epochs (Er​tE_{rt}) in Table 3(a). The default configuration uses an alternating schedule of Es​f​t:Er​t=1:1E_{sft}:E_{rt}=1:1 . We additionally evaluate configurations with increased router updates and stronger expert updates .

Across both OLMoE and Qwen models, we observe that moderate deviations from the default schedule do not improve safety–utility trade-offs. While increasing router updates (1:2) can preserve or slightly improve targeted attack defense in some cases, it often leads to noticeable degradation in cross-attack robustness and general benchmarks. Conversely, increasing expert updates(2:2) tends to destabilize routing behavior, resulting in reduced general performance and higher over-refusal rates. Overall, the balanced (1:1) configuration consistently achieves the best compromise between safety, generalization, and controlled refusal behavior.

5.4 Component Analysis: Expert Alignment, Router Consistency, and Full-Parameter Fine-Tuning

We disentangle the contributions of expert-level alignment and router-level consistency by ablating each component of the bi-level optimization. Specifically, skip-router updates only the identified Safety-Critical Experts while keeping the router fixed, whereas skip-expert optimizes the router without expert fine-tuning. The full framework alternates between both phases.

As shown in Table 3(b), neither component alone is sufficient to achieve robust and generalizable safety. Expert-only alignment (skip-router) effectively suppresses the targeted attack but remains vulnerable to alternative routing paths, leading to degraded cross-attack robustness and increased over-refusal. In contrast, router-only alignment (skip-expert) reduces the activation of known toxic experts but fails to enforce stable refusal behavior once adversaries exploit new routing shortcuts, resulting in severe safety regressions across all attack categories. Only the full alternating strategy consistently achieves high harmlessness across attacks while preserving general utility and maintaining controlled refusal rates, demonstrating that expert alignment and router consistency are complementary and jointly necessary for defense-in-depth.

Full-Parameter Fine-Tuning. As shown in Table 3(c), full-parameter fine-tuning attains high harmlessness across attacks, but at the cost of extreme over-refusal and significant drops in general performance.

5.5 Random Expert Selection

To assess the necessity of activation-based expert identification, we perform an ablation where the same number of experts are selected uniformly at random, rather than based on the activation discrepancy Δl,e\Delta_{l,e}. These randomly selected experts are fine-tuned using the same alignment procedure as in the full framework.

As shown in Table 3(d), random expert selection can yield partial improvements in attack-specific harmlessness. However, this comes at a substantial cost. Across both OLMoE and Qwen, random selection consistently leads to markedly higher over-refusal rates, with XsTest(over-refusal) increasing significantly compared to Adversarial Activation Discrepancy(AAD) selection. In several settings, the model exhibits near-indiscriminate refusal behavior despite high apparent harmlessness.

In addition, random expert alignment degrades general utility. This indicates that randomly modifying experts interferes with benign reasoning pathways, rather than targeting unsafe computation. By contrast, activation-discrepancy-based selection isolates a small set of Safety-Critical Experts that are disproportionately involved in adversarial behavior, enabling effective safety alignment while preserving general capabilities. These results show that principled expert identification is crucial for robust MoE safety alignment.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we identified a fundamental challenge in safety alignment for Mixture-of-Experts language models, where full-parameter fine-tuning can satisfy safety objectives through routing-based shortcuts without correcting the experts responsible for unsafe behavior.

To address this issue, we propose RASA, a routing-aware expert-level alignment framework that explicitly repairs Safety-Critical Experts while preventing routing bypasses through an alternating optimization strategy. Experiments on representative MoE architectures demonstrate that RASA achieves strong and robust defense against diverse jailbreak attacks, supports mixed-attack and multi-turn settings, remains data-efficient, and preserves general model capabilities with controlled over-refusal. These findings highlight the importance of expert-level intervention for robust MoE safety alignment and suggest a general direction for architecture-aware alignment methods that avoid brittle shortcut solutions.
